About

I'm studying Entertainment Technology and Design at UNLV, concentrating in automation and in structural design and rigging. My work sits where engineering meets the shop floor: CAD design, fabrication, mechanical integration, and the systems that keep a show running night after night.

Before UNLV I trained in civil and architectural engineering, which is where I picked up drafting, structural concepts, spatial planning and technical visualization. That foundation still shapes how I work. I design for the person who has to build the thing, not just for the model.

At Universal Horror Unleashed I joined ahead of the August 2025 opening and now handle maintenance across the full property — four immersive haunted houses plus themed areas and restaurants. On a given night that means lighting, scenic, props, special effects, A/V and show control, including Q-SYS. I was promoted from Associate Technician to Venue Maintenance Technician in under a year, and I cross-train with every department that will have me.

Last summer I spent a season at TAIT in Lititz as a Mechanical Integration Intern, working from technical drawings to assemble, modify and test custom staging, rigging and automation for touring productions. I troubleshot fitment and fabrication problems and coordinated with project management, controls, engineering and fabrication. On one stage delivery I co-led a crew of roughly 20 stagehands through the on-site assembly, then trained the tour carpenter on the build so the piece could travel without me.

This fall I joined Allegiant Stadium as a Production Technology Intern, working across show control, audio, video and broadcast for NFL games, concerts and events.

Away from work I'm interested in automotive engineering, immersive experiences and the technical side of film and television. I'm looking for internships now and full-time work after I graduate in December 2027.

Projects

V6 engine model

A working V6 with a turning crankshaft, designed in Fusion and Inventor, then 3D printed and assembled. The block is sectioned so the mechanism stays visible. The hard part was tolerancing — every journal and rod end had to be sized for print shrinkage and layer growth, and still spin freely once the whole assembly came together rather than binding on the first revolution.

Role
Design, print, assembly
Software
Fusion 360, Inventor
Mechanism
Crankshaft, connecting rods, six pistons
Focus
Part tolerancing, alignment, manufacturability

Steve Lacy stage design

A concert stage built around a full-size guitar that doubles as the performance platform. The neck runs out over the deck as an elevated walkway with stairs onto the body, so the artist can work the full width of the stage and still read as the focal point. Amp stacks and minimal signage keep it close to his clean, guitar-driven look, under a trussed roof carrying the lighting rig.

Role
Concept and stage design
Type
Outdoor concert stage, single artist
Features
Elevated neck walkway, scenic amp stacks
Structure
Trussed roof, overhead lighting rig

Crypt — immersive installation

A horror walkthrough designed for a real room rather than an imagined one. I field-measured the space and drew it to its actual dimensions, then laid out a guest path running from an iron gate past candle stands to a coffin and sacrifice table set against a projection wall. Scenic flats stay under 7′4″ so they clear the existing truss, every cable is routed away from the guest path, and the whole build is lightweight and removable so nothing damages the room.

Role
Concept, field survey, drawing set
Drawings
Top view, front and back elevations
Effects
LED uplight, fog and haze, projection, blood pump
Audio
Four subwoofers, distributed speakers
Build
Plywood and plastic sheeting flats, under 7′4″

Chainsaw hand prop

A chainsaw hand prop for a production of The Evil Dead Musical, drawn as a full six-sheet package rather than just a model. The body is built from flat panels so it can be cut and assembled by a shop that isn't me, the blade seats into a slot and is fixed with adhesive and fasteners, and the materials list gives substitutions — MDF or plywood, PVC or acrylic, printed PLA — so it can be built from whatever is on hand.

Role
Design, drafting, build package
Software
Fusion 360
Package
6 sheets, scale 1:7, parts and materials lists
Target
8–12 lb, actor-handled, nightly use

On the floor at Universal

Over a year on the property, and most of this work never gets photographed. It goes in overnight, it has to look like it was always there, and a lot of it I can't show or name. A few things I can.

Scenic

Stone wall, monsters house exit

Built a stone wall in the narrow exit hallway of our monsters house: real stone brick laid over mesh and concrete, running about ten feet to the ceiling. A corridor that tight gives you no room to stand back and read the face as you go, so the courses have to be right on the way up.

Special effects

Flying bat effect

I pitched the idea and the material approach: a pulley run, a drive motor and a collapsible wing mechanism that opens on the travel out and folds on the return, so the bat reads as flight rather than a prop on a wire. The special effects team took it from there and built it into the show.

Repair and redesign

Pneumatic door knocker

A door knocker had torn clean off its wall. Instead of reattaching it we reinforced the mount, changed the design, and brought down the air pressure driving it so the same failure would not come back. Most of my repair work goes that way — fix what caused it, not what broke.

Show systems

Preventative maintenance

Install, operate and troubleshoot lighting fixtures, fog machines and show control under Q-SYS across four haunted houses plus themed areas and restaurants. The work that matters most is the preventative kind: catching the thing that is about to fail during the day instead of during a show.

Other projects

Linear actuator stage lift

A stage-lift prototype drawn in Inventor and 3D printed on a short timeline, driven by a DC motor. Three parts — base, guide rods, stage — with the drawing set carrying the part list and build notes.

DC drive, rapid iteration

Circus wagon

A kinetic wagon built from laser-cut panels with lettering cut into the side rails, barred sides, and running gear underneath. Designed, cut and assembled by hand, then refined until the motion ran true.

Laser cut, running gear

Claw grabber

A working grabber that lifts a metal ball, built entirely from workshop scrap. Grip, leverage and jaw alignment solved inside whatever was already on the rack.

Block and tackle

A laser-cut wooden pulley system that lifts 60 lb, built to demonstrate mechanical advantage while holding its alignment under real load.

Pirate lock box

Layered woodworking with a custom lid mechanism driven by a rotating wheel, so the scenic detail and the moving part were designed as one piece.

Knight helmet

A wearable helmet cut, formed and fastened from sheet metal, with ventilation and sightlines worked in so it could actually be worn.
